title: Caching And Performance Drill
intro: Twelve scenario questions on caching layers, ElastiCache, VPC endpoints and Lambda networking. Answer cold — the explanation appears after each choice.
footer: Drawn from Lab 09 — Cache-aside, measured. Reference notes: exam-notes.md
notes_intro: Twelve SAA-C03-style questions on caching strategy, ElastiCache and private connectivity, then the traps and reference tables. Answers are at the bottom — try them cold first.

questions.q: A Lambda function is attached to a VPC so it can reach an ElastiCache cluster. It must also read from DynamoDB. What is the cheapest way to give it that access?
options: A NAT gateway in a public subnet
A DynamoDB gateway endpoint in the private route table
An interface endpoint for DynamoDB in each subnet
An internet gateway with a public IP on the function
questions.why: A gateway endpoint is free — it is a prefix-list route, not an ENI — and exists for exactly two services: S3 and DynamoDB. A NAT gateway would cost $0.059/hour to send AWS traffic out to the internet and back. Interface endpoints bill hourly per AZ. Lambda functions cannot have public IPs.

questions.q: An application caches query results in Redis with a 60-second TTL. What does the TTL primarily control?
options: How much memory the cache may use
The maximum time a reader may see data that no longer matches the database
How long a client waits before timing out
How frequently the cache replicates to its replica
questions.why: The TTL is the staleness bound — the contract about how out of date an answer may be. Choosing it is a business decision, not a technical one: how wrong can this value be before it matters? Memory pressure is handled separately by the eviction policy.

questions.q: A team needs a cache supporting replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, sorted sets for a leaderboard, and pub/sub. Which engine fits?
options: Memcached
Redis
DynamoDB DAX
CloudFront
questions.why: Redis supports replication, Multi-AZ failover, persistence, transactions and rich data structures including sorted sets and pub/sub. Memcached is a simple multi-threaded key/value cache with no persistence, replication or failover. Leaderboards, pub/sub and high availability all point to Redis.

questions.q: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens when the cache becomes unavailable?
options: The application fails, because the cache is on the critical path
Requests fall through to the database — slower, but still correct
Writes are queued until the cache returns
The database is bypassed and stale data is served
questions.why: In cache-aside the application checks the cache and falls back to the system of record on a miss — so a cache outage costs latency and a burst of database load, never data. A cache whose failure takes the service down is not a cache; it is a dependency, and that is a design error.

questions.q: A DynamoDB-backed application needs microsecond read latency without changing application code. What should be used?
options: ElastiCache for Redis in front of DynamoDB
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
A CloudFront distribution over the API
DynamoDB on-demand capacity
questions.why: DAX is a DynamoDB-specific, write-through cache that is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so it requires essentially no code change and delivers microsecond reads. ElastiCache would work but requires implementing cache-aside yourself. On-demand capacity is a billing mode and changes nothing about latency.

questions.q: Why does attaching a Lambda function to a VPC potentially limit its concurrency?
options: VPC functions are capped at 100 concurrent executions
Each concurrent execution needs an elastic network interface, so subnet IP space becomes a limit
VPC functions may only run in one availability zone
The VPC's route table limits concurrent connections
questions.why: A VPC-attached function runs behind ENIs in your subnets, and those consume IP addresses. Undersized subnets therefore become a hard ceiling on concurrency — a genuine production surprise. Modern Lambda shares ENIs far more efficiently than it once did, but address planning still matters.

questions.q: Which statement about putting a Lambda function in a VPC is correct?
options: It improves security when calling S3 and DynamoDB
It should only be done when the function must reach resources that exist only in the VPC
It is required for any function handling sensitive data
It gives the function a public IP address
questions.why: S3, DynamoDB, SQS and most AWS services are not in your VPC, and a function calling them is no safer inside one. Attaching a VPC costs internet access (unless you add NAT), consumes ENIs and subnet addresses, and adds complexity. Do it only to reach RDS, ElastiCache or other VPC-only resources.

questions.q: An ElastiCache node fails and the cache is empty when it returns. Every request now misses and hits the database simultaneously. What is this called, and what mitigates it?
options: Cache poisoning — mitigated by shorter TTLs
A thundering herd or cache stampede — mitigated by Multi-AZ replicas and staggered TTLs
Cache eviction — mitigated by a larger node
A cold start — mitigated by provisioned concurrency
questions.why: An empty cache sending every request to the database at once is a thundering herd. Mitigations: a replica with automatic failover so the cache is never wholly lost, jittered TTLs so entries do not expire together, and request coalescing so only one caller repopulates a given key.

questions.q: Which caching layer is appropriate for caching whole HTTP responses close to end users worldwide?
options: ElastiCache for Redis
CloudFront
DynamoDB DAX
An Application Load Balancer
questions.why: CloudFront caches HTTP responses at roughly 600 edge locations, close to users. ElastiCache caches arbitrary application data beside the application, in one region. DAX caches DynamoDB items specifically. Load balancers distribute requests; they do not cache.

questions.q: A read-heavy RDS database is CPU-saturated. The application cannot be changed to use a cache. What is the most appropriate scaling action?
options: Enable Multi-AZ
Add read replicas and direct read traffic to them
Enable point-in-time recovery
Increase the backup retention period
questions.why: Read replicas add read capacity — that is precisely what they are for. Multi-AZ adds a standby that serves no traffic and solves availability, not scale. Directing reads at replicas still requires an application or proxy change, but it is the only listed option that adds capacity.

questions.q: Which two AWS services support gateway VPC endpoints?
options: S3 and DynamoDB
S3 and RDS
DynamoDB and SQS
All AWS services support them
questions.why: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB. They are free, implemented as prefix-list routes in a route table rather than as network interfaces, and cannot be reached from on-premises over VPN or Direct Connect. Every other service uses interface endpoints (PrivateLink), which bill hourly per AZ but do work over Direct Connect.

questions.q: An ElastiCache cluster's memory fills up. What determines which items are removed?
options: Items are never removed; writes fail instead
The eviction policy, commonly least-recently-used among keys with a TTL
The oldest items by creation date, always
Items are moved to disk automatically
questions.why: The eviction policy decides — typically volatile-lru (least recently used among keys that have a TTL) or allkeys-lru. A cluster with no eviction policy and no free memory will start rejecting writes, which looks like an application bug rather than a capacity problem.
